definition: A regularization technique that randomly disables a fraction of neurons during training to prevent overfitting.
details: By forcing the network to not rely on any single neuron, dropout encourages redundancy and more robust feature representations, improving generalization to unseen data.

explainer.lead: Dropout is a simple but powerful trick that makes neural networks less likely to memorize their training data. It works by randomly turning off pieces of the network during practice, forcing it to learn more flexible, reliable patterns.

tiers.eli5: Imagine you're practicing for a trivia team, but each round a few teammates are randomly told to sit out. You can't rely on any one person knowing all the answers, so everyone has to learn a bit of everything. Dropout does the same thing for a neural network's neurons — it randomly mutes some during training so the whole team gets stronger.
tiers.practitioner: Dropout is applied during training by zeroing out neurons with a fixed probability, typically 0.2–0.5, using a Bernoulli mask. At test time, all neurons are active but their outputs are scaled by the keep probability (or equivalently, weights are scaled at training time in inverted dropout). Common pitfalls: applying dropout at inference, using too high a rate in small networks, or combining it with batch normalization without care, as the two can interact poorly.
tiers.paperLevel: Dropout is a regularization method where, during each training iteration, each unit in a layer is retained with probability p (the 'keep probability') and otherwise set to zero. The output y of a layer with dropout is y = m * f(x), where m ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise and f is the activation function. At test time, the expected output is approximated by using the full network with weights scaled by p (or by scaling during training in the 'inverted' variant).

explainer.example: A fully-connected layer with 100 neurons uses dropout with p=0.5. In one training batch, neurons 3, 7, 12, and 89 (among 50 total) are randomly zeroed out; the surviving 50 have their outputs doubled. The network must classify an image correctly using only this random subset. Over thousands of batches, every neuron learns to contribute usefully in diverse combinations.

usedIn.name: Convolutional neural networks for image classification
usedIn.detail: Applied after fully-connected layers to reduce overfitting on datasets like ImageNet

usedIn.name: Large language model pre-training
usedIn.detail: Used in transformer architectures to stabilize training on massive text corpora

usedIn.name: Medical imaging models
usedIn.detail: Helps generalize when training data is limited relative to model capacity

explainer.intuition: A network that can solve a problem even when half its neurons are missing has learned robust, distributed representations rather than fragile shortcuts.
howItWorks: During each forward pass of training, randomly select a fraction of neurons to deactivate
Set those neurons' outputs to zero and skip their backward pass for this iteration
Scale the remaining active neurons' outputs to maintain expected magnitude
At test time, use all neurons with appropriately scaled weights (or scale during training)
Repeat this random sampling every batch, creating an ensemble of thinned sub-networks
explainer.whyItMatters: Dropout dramatically reduces overfitting without requiring changes to the loss function or heavy computation, and it approximates training an exponential ensemble of smaller networks at no extra cost.
misconceptions: Dropout should be used during inference — it should not; use all neurons with scaling
Higher dropout rates always help — rates near 1.0 can prevent learning entirely
Dropout and batch normalization always work well together — they can conflict because dropout shifts variance differently at train and test time

diagram.caption: During training, a random mask thins the layer and surviving outputs are scaled before passing onward.

citation.title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting
